title: FICTIONAL EXAMPLE: Daily walking and sleep quality in adults: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This is a fictional abstract written only to demonstrate the carousel pipeline; it does not describe a real study. Poor sleep quality is common among adults.
METHODS: We pooled 12 randomized controlled trials including 1,480 adults aged 30 to 65 years. Participants walked 30 minutes per day for 8 to 12 weeks or continued usual activity. The primary outcome was the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), where lower scores indicate better sleep.
RESULTS: Walking improved sleep quality compared with usual activity (mean difference -1.8 PSQI points, 95% CI -2.4 to -1.2). Time to fall asleep was 9 minutes shorter in walking groups. Effects were similar in men and women. Eight of the 12 trials were conducted in Europe or North America, and only 2 trials were at low risk of bias. No trial followed participants for longer than 12 weeks.
CONCLUSIONS: Walking 30 minutes per day may modestly improve sleep quality in adults, but longer and higher-quality trials are needed.
